paragraphs: This paper examines why neural networks tend to learn simpler image features before more complex ones. It separates images into Fourier amplitude information, associated with pairwise pixel correlations, and phase information, associated with edges and higher-order relationships. Experiments show that simple image classifiers initially depend on amplitudes before learning to exploit phases.

To investigate this progression, the authors build a synthetic model that allows amplitudes and phases to be controlled separately while retaining translation invariance. They prove that phase-only classification is difficult for online stochastic gradient descent under isotropic, high-dimensional inputs. The result makes the input assumptions central to understanding the difficulty of learning these features.

The key finding is that power-law spectra can substantially accelerate phase learning even when those spectra provide no classification information themselves. Theory and experiments support this interaction, including simulations with texture data and deep convolutional networks. Thus, an aspect of the input that does not directly distinguish classes can still make useful information easier to learn.
icml-2026-a-fourier-perspective-on-the-l.tldr: Fourier analysis shows how image amplitude structure can accelerate learning of phase information even without directly helping classification.

paragraphs: This paper investigates hallucinations that occur even when a language model possesses the relevant factual knowledge. That observation suggests that unreliable access to knowledge, rather than missing knowledge alone, can produce incorrect answers. The authors study this instability by examining multiple responses generated for the same prompt.

Their framework, APORIA, represents those responses as points in sentence-embedding space. Its central hypothesis is that factual responses form tighter groups than hallucinated responses. The authors empirically support this hypothesis and report consistent separation between the two classes after Fisher projection. The approach uses patterns across responses to reveal information that a single answer might not expose.

APORIA-LP turns this geometric structure into a label-propagation method for classifying large response collections. Across ten small language models, it achieves F1 scores above 90% using as few as 30–50 annotations. The authors also release 300,000 labelled responses. These findings support geometry as a complementary perspective on hallucination detection, alongside approaches focused on knowledge or individual answers.
icml-2026-a-geometric-analysis-of-small-.tldr: Repeated answers exhibit geometric patterns that help identify hallucinations in small language models using relatively few annotations.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a compact theorem-proving agent intended to make comparisons between AI proof systems more systematic. It includes three capabilities shared by leading approaches: refining proofs over repeated attempts, searching a mathematical library, and managing the context available to the language model. These capabilities form a simple reference architecture.

The authors evaluate the agent across qualitatively different benchmarks, using several frontier language models and alternative design choices. They report performance competitive with leading approaches despite a substantially simpler architecture and a fraction of their cost. The result suggests that these core agent capabilities can account for strong performance without requiring the full complexity of existing systems.

A separate comparison finds consistent benefits from iterative refinement over generating multiple independent, single-shot proof attempts. The advantages are particularly clear in sample efficiency and cost effectiveness. The open-source implementation is offered both as an accessible prover and as a candidate research reference, helping future studies compare model and architecture choices within a shared framework.
icml-2026-a-minimal-agent-for-automated-.tldr: A simple theorem-proving agent achieves competitive results at lower cost, with iterative refinement outperforming repeated single-shot attempts.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether successful attacks on machine-text detectors actually remove the signals that distinguish generated writing. The authors examine attacks ranging from prompt changes to detector-guided optimization. Although these approaches weaken standard detectors, the experiments show that recognizable stylistic patterns can remain in the resulting text.

Few-shot detectors operating on stylistic features remain robust to these attacks, including text from models explicitly tuned to avoid detection. However, the authors also test whether style provides a universal defense. They introduce a paraphrasing approach that jointly seeks undetectability and conformity to particular human writing styles. This approach evades every detector considered, including the style-based ones.

The successful evasion still has a boundary: as more documents become available for analysis, differences between the human and machine distributions reappear. The findings therefore distinguish hiding signals in individual documents from making collections of generated text indistinguishable. They suggest that reliable detection may require examining multiple documents together, rather than relying exclusively on judgments about isolated texts.
icml-2026-attacks-on-machine-text-detect.tldr: Style-aware attacks evade the tested text detectors, but detectable differences reappear when larger document collections are analyzed.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses a large training collection into a small synthetic one while aiming to preserve model performance. This paper identifies a security weakness in attention-based distillation for Transformer text classifiers. Its Attention Hijacking attack manipulates the distillation process so that synthetic data can implant a backdoor through the target model’s attention mechanism.

The authors propose a Semantic Anchoring Hypothesis to explain why the attack can preserve ordinary classification performance. When a trigger aligns with meaningful concepts in the task domain, the attack and the normal task can reinforce each other. In these cases, the reported attack success exceeds 99%, while clean test accuracy also improves.

For functional or noise triggers, the method instead separates attention in a way that avoids the utility collapse observed with baseline attacks. Experiments across several datasets and models from BERT-Tiny to BERT-Base support the attack’s effectiveness and scalability. The security implication is that strong clean accuracy does not, in these experiments, reveal whether a distilled dataset has implanted unwanted behavior.
icml-2026-attention-hijacking-backdoorin.tldr: Attention-based text distillation can carry backdoors that preserve, and sometimes improve, ordinary classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion language models can generate several tokens at once, improving decoding efficiency. However, training objectives focused on individual tokens do not fully address whether those tokens form a coherent sequence together. This paper targets the resulting quality loss when generation becomes more parallel.

The proposed ME-DLM framework first produces a complete response and then applies lightweight corrections. It can replace, delete, or insert tokens while considering the entire sequence. Training targets come from edit distance, with a fixed canonicalization scheme making the correction signal deterministic. This gives the model explicit supervision for minimal changes informed by the surrounding response.

The authors report improved quality and robustness in multi-token parallel generation. Built on LLaDA, ME-DLM gains 11.6 points on HumanEval and 33.6 points on GSM8K while using one-eighth of the total diffusion steps. The findings support post-editing as a way to address sequence consistency while retaining the efficiency benefits of generating many tokens in parallel.
icml-2026-edit-based-refinement-for-para.tldr: ME-DLM improves parallel diffusion generation by making small, globally informed edits after an initial response is complete.

paragraphs: Federated language-model fine-tuning must combine learning from clients whose data distributions differ substantially. This paper argues that model-level remedies often miss these underlying differences. It first introduces Federated Self-Distillation, which smooths client representations into a space aligned with the model’s understanding, and reports improvements over conventional algorithms.

The authors also identify a trade-off: unrestricted self-distillation can increase hallucinations and repetition. They call this the Rewrite Paradox. Their extended method, FedSDR, addresses it with two parallel low-rank adaptation branches. A local smoothing branch learns from distilled data, while a rectification branch remains anchored to the original data to support factual correctness.

Only the rectification branch is aggregated across clients. This design assigns the handling of local distribution differences and the construction of the shared model to different learning streams. The experiments report superior performance for the resulting framework. The contribution is therefore both a strategy for reducing heterogeneity and a correction mechanism for the factual and redundancy problems that the strategy itself can introduce.
icml-2026-fedsdr-federated-self-distilla.tldr: FedSDR combines local self-distillation with a raw-data rectification branch to address federated data differences while protecting factual fidelity.

paragraphs: Multimodal federated learning combines clients that may differ in available modalities, data distributions, and dataset sizes. Choosing which clients participate can therefore shape how training progresses. This paper argues that selection based only on current observations can perform poorly when these training dynamics change quickly.

FedSSM uses decision-aware state space models to predict how candidate participation choices affect future training. Differences between predicted and observed behavior produce a surprise signal that represents uncertainty. The method uses this signal to adjust participation budgets and the balance between exploration and exploitation, comparing possible actions through counterfactual reasoning.

The same signal also informs aggregation. FedSSM combines trust weighting with routing specific to each modality, using surprise to calibrate sensitivity to anomalous clients. Across four multimodal benchmarks, the authors report accuracy improvements of 2.5–4.5% over leading methods and more than 30% fewer communication rounds. These results support coordinating client selection and aggregation around anticipated training behavior, rather than treating participation as a reaction to the present state alone.
icml-2026-fedssm-state-space-model-based.tldr: FedSSM predicts the effects of client participation to improve multimodal federated learning accuracy and reduce communication.

paragraphs: Optimizers such as Muon and Scion use a Linear Minimization Oracle framework and have shown practical advantages for neural-network training. This paper focuses on a mismatch between their implementation and existing theory. Earlier analyses overlook their layer-by-layer operation and use a smoothness assumption that leads to impractically small step sizes.

The authors introduce Gluon, a broader framework that includes previously analyzed methods as special cases. They also develop a refined generalized smoothness model that reflects the geometry of individual network layers. Together, these changes make the analysis more closely match how the optimizers are actually applied and yield state-of-the-art convergence guarantees.

Experiments with NanoGPT and convolutional neural networks support the proposed assumption along the observed optimization trajectories. This empirical check matters because the theoretical improvement depends on a model of how the objective behaves during training. The contribution is a closer connection between practical layer-wise optimization and convergence analysis, supported by evidence that the new assumption describes the tested training runs.
icml-2026-from-muon-to-gluon-bridging-th.tldr: Gluon provides layer-aware theory for LMO-based optimizers, with a refined smoothness assumption supported by training experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies agents that explore an unknown environment before receiving an external reward objective. In reward-free exploration, the collected information must support a near-optimal policy for any later reward. In reward-agnostic exploration, it only needs to support rewards from a small finite collection. The setting is episodic, finite-horizon Markov decision processes.

For the reward-agnostic case, an existing optimal sample-complexity result applies only under a restrictive requirement on the accuracy parameter. The authors propose an algorithm that substantially relaxes that requirement. It uses an online learning procedure with carefully constructed rewards to build an exploration policy, then gathers data for estimating the environment’s dynamics.

Once the external reward is revealed, those dynamics estimates support computation of a policy within the requested accuracy of optimal performance. The paper separately proves a tight lower bound for reward-free exploration, matching known upper bounds. These contributions clarify both how to explore efficiently for a restricted reward collection and the fundamental exploration cost when any reward may arrive later.
icml-2026-improved-bounds-for-reward-agn.tldr: The paper broadens an efficient reward-agnostic exploration guarantee and closes the known bounds gap for reward-free exploration.

paragraphs: Long simulations of Hamiltonian systems are constrained by the small time steps needed for stable numerical integration. This paper proposes learning how a system evolves over a chosen time interval directly. Its Hamiltonian Flow Maps predict mean evolution in phase space, enabling larger updates than classical integrators can stably support.

The training method imposes a Mean Flow consistency condition on time-averaged Hamiltonian dynamics. Crucially, it can learn from independent phase-space samples without being given their future states. That removes the need to generate expensive trajectories specifically to provide examples of before-and-after evolution, connecting the training objective to information available in isolated samples.

The authors validate the framework across several Hamiltonian systems, with particular benefits for molecular dynamics using machine-learned force fields. They report comparable training and inference costs while supporting substantially larger integration steps. Training directly on available trajectory-free force-field datasets makes the approach relevant to existing data resources as well as to the numerical challenge of advancing simulations efficiently.
icml-2026-learning-hamiltonian-flow-maps.tldr: Learned Hamiltonian Flow Maps enable stable larger simulation steps while training on independent samples without future-state targets.

paragraphs: This paper studies a safety problem in which a benign question about a sensitive subject prompts a model to introduce dangerous information during its reasoning. The authors call this unintended elicitation. Their benchmark experiments find that it is common among the tested reasoning models, whose extended reasoning can explore harmful details beyond what the question requires.

The proposed training approach places models in synthesized, open-ended environments where they can search for ways to reason safely while remaining helpful. A scalable data pipeline generates examples that trigger the problem. A safety-first reward model then prioritizes safety while also evaluating response helpfulness and whether the reasoning remains faithful.

Experiments show improved safety, fewer unnecessary refusals, and strong retained helpfulness. These results matter because avoiding harmful elaboration and answering legitimate questions are both objectives of the method. The work treats safety as something that must persist through the reasoning process, including when the user’s request itself is benign, rather than as a property of the final answer alone.
icml-2026-more-sail-than-ballast-address.tldr: Safety-focused training reduces harmful information introduced during reasoning while preserving helpful answers and reducing over-refusal.

paragraphs: Open-ended answers are difficult to train against a single verifiable reward, while overall human preferences can provide only coarse guidance. Rubrics offer more explicit evaluation criteria, but fixed rubrics can become inadequate as a model changes. They may miss newly emerging problems or leave opportunities for reward-hacking behavior.

OnlineRubrics updates those criteria during training. It compares pairs of responses produced by the current policy and a reference policy, using those comparisons to curate evaluation criteria. This ongoing process allows the training signal to address errors that become visible as learning proceeds, rather than depending entirely on standards fixed before training began.

The authors report consistent improvements over exclusively static rubrics, with gains reaching 8% across the evaluated benchmarks and validation sets. Their qualitative analysis identifies recurring criteria involving transparency, practicality, organization, and reasoning. The findings support adapting the evaluation rubric alongside the model, so that post-training can respond to developing weaknesses in long-form answers.
icml-2026-online-rubrics-elicitation-fro.tldr: OnlineRubrics improves post-training by continually updating evaluation criteria from comparisons of current and reference model responses.

paragraphs: Rényi differential privacy describes privacy through a profile indexed by Rényi order. Another representation expresses privacy as a trade-off between errors in a hypothesis test. This paper asks how tightly the second representation can be inferred when the only available information is the first.

The authors prove that intersecting the privacy regions associated with individual Rényi orders gives an optimal conversion. Equivalently, at each Type I error level, one takes the strongest of the corresponding single-order trade-off bounds. The result applies simultaneously to every valid Rényi privacy profile and every such error level, resolving the stated conjecture.

The proof uses the convex geometry of Rényi privacy regions and a characterization of their boundaries through Bernoulli mechanisms. Its practical meaning is a limit on information recovery: no other black-box conversion can uniformly improve this rule in the stated Blackwell sense using only the same Rényi guarantees. Stronger conclusions about a particular mechanism would therefore require information beyond its Rényi privacy profile.
icml-2026-optimal-conversion-from-renyi-.tldr: Intersecting single-order Rényi privacy regions yields the optimal black-box conversion from an RDP profile to a hypothesis-testing privacy trade-off.

paragraphs: POLCA treats improving prompts and multi-turn agents as an optimization problem in which a language model proposes candidate systems. Numerical scores and written feedback guide that search. The challenge is that evaluations can be noisy, sampled data can vary, and candidate systems can behave stochastically, while the set of possible solutions keeps expanding.

The framework maintains a priority queue containing candidates and their evaluation histories. This supports a balance between exploring alternatives and investing further in promising solutions. An epsilon-net mechanism maintains diversity among candidates, while an LLM summarizer draws lessons from previous trials so that accumulated experience can inform later proposals.

The authors prove convergence to near-optimal candidates under stochasticity and evaluate POLCA on benchmarks spanning several tasks. They report robust performance that is efficient in both samples and time, outperforming the compared state-of-the-art algorithms in deterministic and stochastic settings. Together, these results support managing search history, diversity, and noisy feedback as central components of language-model-driven system optimization.
icml-2026-polca-stochastic-generative-op.tldr: POLCA organizes language-model-driven optimization around candidate priorities, diversity, and summarized experience to handle noisy evaluations efficiently.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian and underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo generate samples by numerically simulating dynamics. Integration errors introduce persistent bias into estimated expectations, which a Metropolis-Hastings adjustment can remove. Omitting that adjustment can improve efficiency in high dimensions, but requires choosing a step size that keeps bias acceptably small.

This paper introduces automatic step-size tuning based on a user-specified asymptotic bias tolerance. The method connects changes in energy during integration to the resulting bias. That relationship provides a way to tune unadjusted sampling without manually selecting a step size, making the trade-off between bias and sampling variance more practical.

The authors rigorously bound the asymptotic bias for Gaussian targets and provide numerical evidence beyond that setting. Comparisons cover Bayesian inference and a statistical physics model with more than one million parameters. With the proposed tuning, unadjusted samplers achieve close to optimal performance and consistently outperform adjusted versions in the reported tests. The distinction between the Gaussian guarantee and broader empirical evidence is central to interpreting the result.
icml-2026-practical-and-scalable-hamilto.tldr: Automatic step-size tuning makes unadjusted Monte Carlo sampling practical, with Gaussian bias guarantees and broader empirical efficiency gains.

paragraphs: Parameter-based knowledge editing changes selected model weights to update stored knowledge. This paper questions whether such localized changes reliably preserve the model’s wider abilities. Its theoretical analysis builds on the dimensional Collapse Hypothesis, describing how edits can spread through fragile directions in representation space and cause interference beyond the intended update.

That analysis links local weight changes to possible global damage and reasoning collapse. The authors then investigate the issue empirically by varying knowledge complexity, the number of edits, evaluation dimensions, and comparison methods. This connects the proposed mechanism to a broader assessment of model behavior after editing, rather than judging an edit solely by whether it changes the targeted fact.

Across the evaluated conditions, parameter-editing methods consistently damage core capabilities. A simple retrieval-based baseline also performs better than every tested parameter-editing method. These findings support making preservation of general model abilities a central evaluation goal. The reported comparison concerns the tested methods and conditions, while the theoretical explanation specifically rests on the stated hypothesis.
icml-2026-revisiting-parameter-based-kno.tldr: The paper links localized knowledge edits to broader interference and finds retrieval stronger than all tested parameter-editing methods.

paragraphs: Dueling optimization seeks better solutions using only comparisons between candidates, without access to numerical objective values. This paper extends that problem to Riemannian manifolds, where the feasible solutions have curved geometry. The extension addresses applications outside the unconstrained Euclidean setting emphasized by earlier work.

The authors introduce Riemannian Dueling Normalized Gradient Descent and establish iteration-complexity guarantees under geodesic smoothness or geodesic convexity assumptions, including strong convexity. These conditions describe the objective along paths appropriate to the manifold. They make the geometry part of the optimization analysis rather than treating solutions as unrestricted points in ordinary flat space.

For settings where projection is prohibited, the paper also develops Riemannian Dueling Frank–Wolfe, a projection-free alternative. It provides bounds on both iterations and comparison-oracle calls. Numerical experiments on synthetic problems and real applications illustrate the effectiveness of the methods. The contribution is therefore a pair of algorithms and associated guarantees for comparison-based optimization under geometric constraints.
icml-2026-riemannian-dueling-optimizatio.tldr: Two Riemannian algorithms extend comparison-only optimization to curved solution spaces, including settings where projection is prohibited.

paragraphs: Group Relative Policy Optimization benefits from varied generated solutions, but adding randomness at each token can produce incoherent reasoning. This paper identifies another source of diversity: smaller models within the same family. As sample counts increase, their stronger pass@k indicates a useful variety of possible solution paths.

The authors characterize this as policy-level diversity that remains correlated across reasoning steps and preserves logical consistency. Their S2L-PO framework uses fixed small models to supply exploration for a larger learner. A progressive annealing strategy gradually shifts training from offline small-model rollouts toward samples generated by the larger model itself.

That transition addresses the smaller model’s capacity limits, which can otherwise cause performance drops partway through training. The authors report faster convergence, improved mathematical reasoning accuracy, and reduced rollout computation. One result is an 8.8% accuracy gain on AIME 24 when a 1.7-billion-parameter explorer guides an 8-billion-parameter learner. The findings support using coherent variation between policies as a training resource beyond token-level randomness.
icml-2026-smaller-models-are-natural-exp.tldr: S2L-PO uses smaller models’ diverse reasoning paths to train larger models, then gradually shifts to the learner’s own samples.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning produces task-specific changes to model parameters, but learning those changes again for every model variant can be expensive. This paper studies transferring such updates between models of different widths. Its method, Theseus, identifies an update through what it does to intermediate representations rather than through a direct correspondence between weights.

The authors formulate transfer as matching the update’s functional effect on observed activations. They first align representation spaces using orthogonal Procrustes analysis. In that aligned setting, they derive a stable closed-form solution that preserves the geometry of the update. This provides a transfer procedure without additional training or backpropagation.

Experiments on vision and language models of different widths show consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines. The results indicate that useful task information can survive differences in parameter dimensions when transfer is organized around representation changes. The supported scope is cross-width transfer: the method demonstrates how functional matching can connect these heterogeneous models without relearning the task update.
icml-2026-transporting-task-vectors-acro.tldr: Theseus transfers task updates between different-width models by matching their effects on representations, without additional training.

paragraphs: Causal Foundation Models aim to combine causal discovery and inference in one reusable model. However, the models considered here cannot incorporate domain knowledge, potentially weakening their predictions. This paper introduces ways to condition them on known causal relationships so that existing expertise can inform their answers.

The supplied knowledge can be a complete causal graph or ancestral information describing which variables lie upstream of others. The approach also accepts partial information, avoiding a requirement to know the entire causal structure. The authors compare conditioning strategies and find that learnable biases added to attention are the most effective way to use both full and incomplete knowledge.

In experiments, this conditioning allows a general-purpose causal model to match specialized models trained for particular causal structures. The result supports combining reusable causal inference with problem-specific expertise. Partial graphs are especially relevant to that goal because the method can make use of available relationships without requiring a complete account of the system before answering causal queries.
icml-2026-use-what-you-know-causal-found.tldr: Conditioning causal foundation models on full or partial causal knowledge lets a general-purpose model match specialized models in experiments.

paragraphs: Adapting a foundation model with only a few examples can work well empirically while offering weak guarantees about performance on unseen data. This paper designs a transfer-learning procedure around obtaining informative generalization certificates. It focuses on parameter-efficient fine-tuning, where adaptation changes a restricted set of model parameters.

The method first learns a distribution over adaptation parameters from upstream tasks using a diffusion model. For a downstream task, it samples candidate adaptations and selects the one with the highest likelihood on the available examples. This sample-and-evaluate procedure restricts the final choice to a finite collection of candidates.

That finite hypothesis set is central to the theory: it enables tighter risk certificates than the usual continuous space of neural-network weights. The authors instantiate their bound and obtain non-trivial guarantees in a low-shot setting where the compared learning approaches yield vacuous bounds. The contribution links how adaptations are proposed and selected to whether their generalization can be meaningfully certified.
icml-2026-weight-space-learning-for-cert.tldr: Sampling a finite set of learned parameter adaptations enables informative generalization guarantees for few-shot transfer learning.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can waste computation by applying lengthy reasoning to simple tasks. Adaptive models try to avoid this by choosing between explicit reasoning and a direct answer. This paper identifies a weakness in that choice: verbose wording can make an easy problem appear difficult, triggering unnecessary computation.

The proposed framework trains the choice in two stages. First, supervised fine-tuning presents simple problems in both concise and redundant forms, teaching the model to separate wording length from task difficulty. A subsequent reinforcement-learning stage uses Group Relative Policy Optimization with a custom reward to refine when the model selects each response mode.

The resulting model reduces computational overhead without sacrificing accuracy and becomes more robust to misleading linguistic complexity. The approach matters because selecting a reasoning mode is itself a decision that needs training. By exposing the model to equivalent problems expressed differently, then refining its selection policy, the method addresses a concrete source of inefficient reasoning rather than merely encouraging shorter answers.
icml-2026-when-simple-problems-wear-comp.tldr: Two-stage training helps adaptive reasoning models avoid unnecessary reasoning when simple problems are phrased verbosely.

paragraphs: This paper examines who reports on the social effects of foundation models and which issues receive attention. The authors analyze 186 developer release reports and 248 third-party evaluation sources, supplemented by developer interviews. Their scope includes bias, fairness, privacy, environmental costs, and labor, extending beyond general capability testing.

The analysis finds an uneven division of work. Developer reporting is often sparse or superficial, with declining attention to areas such as environmental impact and bias. Independent evaluators provide broader and more rigorous coverage of bias, harmful content, and performance disparities. However, developers alone can authoritatively disclose important details about data provenance, moderation labor, costs, and infrastructure.

Interviews suggest that these disclosures receive lower priority unless connected to product adoption or compliance. Independent testing therefore leaves gaps where the necessary information remains with developers. The authors argue for mandatory developer transparency, stronger independent evaluation ecosystems, and shared infrastructure for collecting external assessments. Their findings connect gaps in evaluation coverage to differences in access and reporting incentives.
icml-2026-who-evaluates-ais-social-impac.tldr: Independent evaluators cover many AI social impacts more thoroughly, but major gaps persist in information only developers can disclose.

paragraphs: ZeroBench addresses a problem with visual evaluation: models can score highly on popular benchmarks while still struggling to interpret images and reason spatially. As familiar benchmarks approach saturation, they leave less room to measure further improvement. The authors construct a lightweight benchmark intended to remain challenging for longer.

The benchmark uses adversarial filtering to select visual reasoning questions that frontier multimodal models could not solve at its original release. Initial state-of-the-art scores were zero under both pass@1 and pass@5. The description of the benchmark as impossible therefore refers to those evaluated models at release, rather than a claim that its questions can never be solved.

The study evaluates 46 models, compares them with a human baseline, and tracks progress over the following year. Later nonzero scores demonstrate improvement while leaving substantial remaining headroom. The authors also analyze model strengths and weaknesses and publicly release the benchmark. This combination makes ZeroBench a tool for observing visual capability development beyond benchmarks that already yield high scores.
icml-2026-zerobench-an-impossible-visual.tldr: ZeroBench uses adversarially filtered visual questions to measure progress on tasks that frontier multimodal models initially failed completely.
